title: The Army just used a 20-kilowatt laser to take out three drones
gist: Between the night of August 25 and early August 26 the US Army's Joint Task Force Southern Border used AeroVironment's vehicle-mounted 20-kilowatt Locust Laser Weapon System, derived from the Army's AMP-HEL program, to shoot down three drones in the Rio Grande Valley. JTF-SB commander Curtis Taylor linked the drones to cartel networks conducting smuggling and surveillance, marking an operational deployment of directed energy on US domestic soil.

insights.claim: The US Army used a high-energy multipurpose laser to shoot down three drones near the US-Mexico border between the night of August 25 and the early morning of August 26, in the vicinity of the Rio Grande Valley in Texas, in an operation led by Joint Task Force Southern Border under US Northern Command.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Directed-energy weapons have crossed from test range to operational use on US territory, which typically precedes budget expansion and procurement scale-up.

insights.claim: The engagement used technology derived from the Army's High-Energy Multipurpose Laser (AMP-HEL) program, a military effort focused on fielding high-energy lasers as a new defense capability.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: AMP-HEL is the specific program line to track for follow-on contract awards in counter-UAS directed energy.

insights.claim: AeroVironment delivered the first two functional prototypes of these laser weapons to the US Armed Forces in September 2025 and two further improved systems in December of the same year as the program expanded.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A doubling of delivered units within one quarter is an early sign of a program moving from prototype to production — the inflection that matters for the supplier's revenue.
insights.locator: Available information suggests that this initiative began in September 2025

insights.claim: The Locust Laser Weapon System operates at 20 kilowatts and is designed to be mounted on military vehicles, which is how the Army has fielded the versions it received.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The 20 kW class sets the target set — small drones, not missiles — and defines where the system competes against kinetic and jamming counter-UAS alternatives.

insights.claim: Locust detects and tracks a target using sensors, cameras or radar, focuses a concentrated beam on it even while moving, then applies an additional electrical charge to convert the beam into heat that damages or disables the drone, with outcomes depending on distance, exposure time and target characteristics.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Effectiveness is conditional on dwell time and range rather than binary, which is the key limitation buyers weigh against magazine-depth advantages.

insights.claim: The most recent Locust versions delivered in December include integrated radar and command-and-control systems, allowing the weapon to be embedded in a more complex mobile defense platform rather than used standalone.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Moving from point weapon to networked node raises system value per unit and the barrier to competitor substitution.

themes.theme: Cartel drone threat and policy framing

insights.claim: JTF-SB commander Curtis Taylor said cartel networks are increasingly employing unmanned aircraft systems to facilitate illicit human smuggling and to actively spy on US personnel and law enforcement partners, and framed the laser as part of layered countermeasures.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Non-state actors fielding drones at scale creates a durable domestic demand driver for counter-UAS spending outside traditional overseas theaters.

insights.claim: The exact location of the operation, the origin of the neutralized drones, the entities operating them, and the specific AMP-HEL models used all remain undisclosed.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Thin disclosure means the operational-effectiveness claim cannot be independently verified — treat it as a program milestone announcement rather than validated performance data.

insights.claim: The international press has linked the laser action to the campaign against illegal immigration and drug cartels that President Trump has waged since beginning his second term, with high-energy laser systems being just part of a growing technology toolkit deployed at the border.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Border security is becoming a procurement channel for advanced military technology, broadening the addressable market for defense-tech suppliers beyond foreign conflict.
